newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS - Thai markets end frenzied week on calmer note.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thai markets end frenzied week on calmer note.

text.p: Thai investors heaved a sigh of relief on Friday as the country's stock and money markets finished a frenetic week on a slightly calmer note.

After nearly three weeks of seemingly endless declines and a seven percent drop in the past five trading days, the Stock Exchange of Thailand's key index nudged up slightly to end 3.32 points higher at 561.19.
Afternoon bargain-hunting helped boost the index, brokers said.
Traders and analysts said the bourse was buoyed by feelings that the latest currency crisis was over, and belief that the Thai baht was not going to be devalued in the near term.

"The foreigners are coming in, picking up cheap stocks. Once it became clear that the baht was not going to be devalued, at least during this current round, on valuations there are cheap stocks here," said a foreign trader.

The baht, which was hammered on Wednesday and Thursday amid rumours of an imminent devaluation, remained relatively steady throughout the day. It was quoted at 25.775/25.865 bid/ask to the dollar in late deals after falling as low as 26.330/26.430 late on Wednesday when speculators aggressively dumped the baht.
The central bank said on Friday that speculative attacks on the baht had ended and the situation for the embattled currency was returning to normal.
"Since yesterday, there has been no speculation (in the baht). If there is any speculation, we will do our duty (and intervene)," said Bank of Thailand deputy governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi.

The Bank of Thailand teamed with several regional central banks this week and intervened in foreign exchange markets to successfully defend the baht. It also asked local banks not to buy dollars from offshore parties in another attempt to fend off speculation in the baht.

Analysts cautioned that although markets had stabilised on Friday, the fundamental problem behind the crisis -- a slowing economy and a lack of confidence that the government's current measures will be able to cure it -- still remains.

"I think it is a victory but not the end of the war," said George Morgan, country manager for ABM-AMRO Hoare Govett. "It's not backed up by any improvement in economic outlook. Speculators will be back again."
Thai authorities said they would announce on Monday some support measures to try and help the battered stock market, which is at eight-year lows.

Those measures include the issue of 5.0 billion baht ($192 million) bonds by Securities Finance Corp (SFC), which will use the funds to buy margin loans from securities companies, central bank assistant governor Siri Ganjarerndee said on Friday.

Traders and analysts said a slew of first quarter corporate results released on Friday were generally negative, but said a decline in earnings had already been widely anticipated. Most results came in above worst case forecasts, they said.
"They were almost all poor, very poor, but predictably so," said an analyst at a leading European broker.
